sections.title: 1. Purpose and place in the outline

blocks.text: Grade 3 is the year grammar becomes formal (§3A): mastery of the parts of speech, sentence diagramming, and the first steps toward the paragraph. It is also the year the progymnasmata begins, with stage 1, the fable: the student retells a fable in their own words, then expands it, condenses it, and changes its point of view (§3A). This is the first rung of the composition ladder that ends in a defended senior thesis.

The course has two halves that share a week: grammar, which names the parts of a sentence, and composition, which builds sentences into a story. Each feeds the other. A child who can find the verb can fix a sentence that has none.

The progymnasmata says to retell a fable the student already knows. So this course does not introduce fables of its own. It uses the Aesop fables Literature (01) reads in task C, each one week after Literature has read it. If Literature reads The Lion and the Mouse in week 1, Grammar & Composition works with it in week 2.
This settles the "check against 02" question left open in the Literature manuals: the two courses share one fable list of 35, and Literature always reads a fable first.

terms.title: Grammar: the sentence, nouns, verbs · Composition: Retell the fable

head: Grammar
What a sentence is; four kinds of sentences; nouns (common and proper); action verbs; subject and predicate
rows: Simple subject and verb on the baseline
Progymnasmata stage 1, first operation: retell a fable faithfully, every event in order, in 4–6 sentences
From Literature, one week behind: The Lion and the Mouse (wk 2), The Tortoise and the Hare (wk 3), The Ant and the Grasshopper (wk 4), The Crow and the Pitcher (wk 5), The Boy Who Cried Wolf (wk 6)
Drawn from Literature Term 1: Pocahontas, the Pilgrims, Sarah Noble

glance.text: Order each week. A before B. C before D, in different sittings, with D at least a day later so the draft can cool. The two pairs can be done in any order.

blocks.text: Draw a horizontal baseline. Write the simple subject on the left and the verb on the right, separated by a vertical line that crosses the baseline.
Pilgrims | sailed

In Term 1 only the subject and verb go on the diagram, even when the sentence has more words. In "The tired Pilgrims sailed across the sea," the diagram is still Pilgrims | sailed. The other words find their places in Terms 2 and 4. Commanding sentences have an understood subject, written (you).
The child checks each line of the draft and fixes what's wrong, then makes a clean copy.
1. Every sentence starts with a capital letter.
2. Every sentence ends with the right mark (. ? !).
3. Every sentence is complete: it has a subject and a verb.
4. Names of people and places have capital letters.
5. All the fable's events are there, in order.
Lines 3 and 4 are added as they're taught, in weeks 1 and 3. The parent circles misspelled words, and the child corrects them in the clean copy. Spelling isn't scored.
Definition to say back: "A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought. It begins with a capital letter and ends with a punctuation mark."
Model: "Pocahontas lived in a village." It's a complete thought. "In a village" is not: who? what happened?
Diagram: Pocahontas | lived.
Sentence or not? Mark each one S or N, and fix each N into a sentence:
1. The ships came across the ocean.
2. Across the ocean.
3. Sarah walked through the forest.
4. Her father and the horse.
5. John Smith explored the river.
6. Very cold and dark.
Diagram: Pocahontas laughed. · Ships arrived. · The settlers worked.
Dictation: "The ships came from England. They sailed for many weeks."
No fable yet. Write five complete sentences about your own morning, each starting with a capital and ending with a period.
Checklist lines 1–3. Clean copy.
Definition to say back: "A declarative sentence makes a statement. An interrogative sentence asks a question. An imperative sentence gives a command. An exclamatory sentence shows strong feeling."
Models:
"The mouse helped the lion." (declarative .)
"Did the mouse help the lion?" (interrogative ?)
"Help the lion." (imperative .)
"The mouse saved the lion!" (exclamatory !)
Diagram the command: (you) | Help.
Label each D, Int, Imp or E and add the end mark:
1. Sarah was afraid of the dark
2. Keep up your courage
3. Where is my father
4. What a huge forest this is
5. The Pilgrims prayed together
6. Look at the river
Diagram: Sarah listened. · Come here. (understood you) · Ships waited.
Dictation: "Keep up your courage, Sarah. Where is the trail?"

Draft — retell The Lion and the Mouse. Without the book, retell the fable in 4–6 sentences. Begin with the lion catching the mouse and end with the mouse setting him free. Include one question or one exclamation somewhere.
Checklist lines 1–3 and 5. Clean copy.
Definition to say back: "A noun names a person, place, thing or idea. A common noun names any one of a kind. A proper noun names a particular one and begins with a capital letter."
Models: girl / Sarah; ship / Mayflower; town / Plymouth; courage (an idea).
Diagram: "Squanto taught." becomes Squanto | taught.
Underline every noun, and circle the proper nouns:
1. The Pilgrims left England on a ship.
2. Sarah and her father built a house in Connecticut.
3. Pocahontas brought corn to the settlers.
4. The children played in the forest.
5. Courage helped Sarah.
Capitalize the proper nouns: john smith · jamestown · the mayflower · england.
Diagram: Squanto taught. · Sarah cooked. · The Mayflower sailed.
Dictation: "Sarah lived in Connecticut. Her father built a house."
Draft — retell The Tortoise and the Hare. 4–6 sentences, from the challenge to the finish. Name the two animals as characters. Use "Tortoise" and "Hare" as their names, with capitals.
Checklist lines 1–5. Line 4 is new this week. Clean copy.
Definition to say back: "A verb shows action or being. An action verb tells what someone or something does."
Models: sail, plant, run, pray, shout. Test: can you put I or they in front of it? "They sail." Yes, it's a verb.
Diagram: "The grasshopper sang." becomes grasshopper | sang.
Circle the action verb in each sentence:
1. The ant carried grain.
2. The settlers planted corn.
3. Sarah's father chopped wood.
4. The children ran into the forest.
5. The Pilgrims landed at Plymouth.
6. The wind blew all night.
Write three sentences of your own about the Pilgrims, each with a different action verb.
Diagram: The ant worked. · The grasshopper played. · Winter came.
Dictation: "The ant worked all summer. The grasshopper sang and played."
Draft — retell The Ant and the Grasshopper. 4–6 sentences, from summer to winter. Choose strong action verbs: hauled instead of got, begged instead of asked.
Checklist 1–5, plus: circle the verbs in your draft. Is there one in every sentence? Clean copy.
Definition to say back: "Every sentence has two parts. The subject tells whom or what the sentence is about. The predicate tells what the subject does or is."
How to find them:
1. Find the verb first.
2. Ask "who or what ___?" The answer is the simple subject.
3. The complete subject is all the words that go with it; the complete predicate is the verb and all the words that go with it.
Model: "The thirsty crow | dropped pebbles into the pitcher." The verb is dropped. Who dropped? crow. The simple subject is crow; the complete subject is the thirsty crow.
Diagram: crow | dropped.
Draw a line between the complete subject and the complete predicate. Then underline the simple subject once and the verb twice:
1. The brave girl slept in the forest.
2. A kind Native woman fed Sarah.
3. The Pilgrim children gathered nuts.
4. The cold winter killed many settlers.
5. Squanto showed the Pilgrims a trick with fish.
Diagram (subject and verb only): The thirsty crow thought. · Many Pilgrims died. · The clever bird drank.
Dictation: "The thirsty crow found a pitcher. The water was low."
Draft — retell The Crow and the Pitcher. 4–6 sentences. Make sure the crow's idea is clear: what he did, and why it worked.
Checklist 1–5. For one sentence in your draft, mark the subject and predicate. Clean copy.

weeks.title: Review, term check and marked fable

blocks.text: The child says all five definitions back: sentence, four kinds, noun, verb, subject and predicate. Diagram together: The Pilgrims prayed. · Listen. · Pocahontas smiled.
Done independently, in one sitting, about 25 minutes. Answer key below.
Draft — retell The Boy Who Cried Wolf. 4–6 sentences, from the first false cry to the real wolf.
Checklist 1–5, then a clean copy. The parent marks the clean copy on the rubric below and files it in the portfolio.
Part 1 — Identify (10 items, one point each).
1–2. Label the kind of sentence: (1) "Where did the ships land?" (2) "Plant the corn now."
3–5. Underline the nouns in "The Pilgrims built houses in Plymouth." (three nouns, one point each)
6. Which noun in item 3–5 is proper?
7–8. Circle the verb: (7) "The settlers worked hard." (8) "Sarah sang to the children."
9–10. Mark the complete subject: (9) "The little mouse ran away." (10) "A big ship sailed into the bay."
Part 2 — Diagram (5 sentences, subject and verb only).
1. Squanto helped.
2. The hare slept.
3. The tired Pilgrims rested.
4. Run!
5. Pocahontas walked to Jamestown.
Answer key.
Part 1: 1 interrogative · 2 imperative · 3–5 Pilgrims, houses, Plymouth · 6 Plymouth · 7 worked · 8 sang · 9 The little mouse · 10 A big ship.
Part 2: 1 Squanto | helped · 2 hare | slept · 3 Pilgrims | rested · 4 (you) | Run · 5 Pocahontas | walked.

Mastery gate: 8 of 10 in Part 1 and 4 of 5 in Part 2. Below the gate in either part, Term 2 week 7 becomes a review week, repeating whichever lessons were missed, and Term 2's new material starts in week 8. Record the scores.
Score each line 0, 1 or 2, for six points in all. Record the score, not a letter grade.

rows: Every event in order: the false cries, the villagers coming, the real wolf, no one coming
Complete sentences, correct capitals and end marks

blocks.text: 4 or more is on track. Below 4, Term 2 keeps the same 4–6 sentence length and adds the moral sentence a week later than planned.
Keep lessons short. The lesson (A) should take 25–30 minutes, not an hour (§2, multum non multa). If the child has the definition and two diagrams, stop.
Definitions are memory work. Add each week's definition to the Memory Work queue (11) so the daily core drills it.
Don't fix the draft during task C. The child writes the draft without help, and corrections happen in D, from the checklist. That's the whole reason for the cooling day.
Dictation: read each sentence twice, then once more while the child checks. Correct together afterward. It isn't a test.
Print the revision checklist and keep it by the child's writing place
Add the five definitions to the Memory Work queue as they're taught
Make sure Literature reads each fable the week before it's retold here
Week 6: give the term check, mark the fable, record both scores and file the clean copy in the portfolio

terms.title: Grammar: adjectives, articles, adverbs, plurals and possessives · Composition: Retell + moral

head: Grammar
Adjectives; articles; adverbs; plural nouns; possessive nouns
rows: Adjectives, articles and possessives on slanted lines under the noun; adverbs on slanted lines under the verb
Retell the fable, then state its moral in your own words as the final sentence. 5–7 sentences

From Literature, one week behind: The Dog and His Reflection (wk 7), The Fox and the Grapes (wk 8), The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse (wk 9), The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs (wk 10), The North Wind and the Sun (wk 11), The Fox and the Crow (wk 12)
Drawn from Literature Term 2: Ben Franklin, Ox-Cart Man, Amos the mouse

glance.text: If the child was below the Term 1 gate. Week 7 becomes a review week: repeat the Term 1 lessons that were missed (task A) and redo the missed parts of the term check (task B). The composition tasks in week 7 go ahead as written. Then teach weeks 7–9 in weeks 8–10, skip week 10 (the flex week), and carry on from week 11. Nothing new is lost: week 10 only combines earlier lessons.
Order each week. A before B. C before D, in different sittings, with D at least a day later. The two pairs can be done in any order.

blocks.text: Words that describe hang on slanted lines below the word they describe.
Adjectives, articles and possessive nouns go under the noun.
Adverbs go under the verb.
"The young printer worked hard." becomes:
printer | worked
\The \young \hard
Read the diagram back aloud: printer worked; which printer? the young one; worked how? hard. Words not yet taught (prepositional phrases, objects) still stay off the diagram until Terms 3 and 4.
1. Every sentence starts with a capital letter.
2. Every sentence ends with the right mark (. ? !).
3. Every sentence is complete: it has a subject and a verb.
4. Names of people and places have capital letters.
5. All the fable's events are there, in order.
6. New: The last sentence states the moral in your own words.
7. New from week 7: At least two adjectives that tell what kind. From week 9: at least one adverb that tells how.
The parent circles misspelled words, and the child corrects them in the clean copy. Spelling isn't scored.

Teach this once, in week 7 task C. A moral is the fable's lesson for people, not for animals. Test: could it be true for a boy, a farmer or a king? "The dog lost his bone" is not a moral. "If you're greedy, you can lose what you already have" is.
Literature gave each fable's moral in a child's words. The student should not copy that line. Ask them to say the moral their own way first, out loud, before writing.
Definition to say back: "An adjective describes a noun or pronoun. It tells what kind, which one, how many, or whose."
Models: busy street (what kind) · that kite (which one) · three loaves (how many). In "The wise old man wrote sayings," wise and old describe man.
Diagram: man | wrote, with wise and old on slants under man.
Circle each adjective and draw an arrow to the noun it describes:
1. Ben bought three puffy rolls.
2. The tired farmer walked to the busy market.
3. A small mouse lived in the fur cap.
4. The ox pulled a heavy cart.
5. Ben was a clever boy.
Add two adjectives to each: The kite flew. · The cart rolled. · The printer worked.
Diagram: Clever Ben laughed. · The heavy cart creaked. · Small Amos squeaked.
Dictation: "Ben carried three large rolls. He walked down the busy street."

Draft — retell The Dog and His Reflection, with a moral. 5–7 sentences. Describe the bone and the water with at least two adjectives. End with the moral in your own words. Teach "How to state a moral" first.
Checklist 1–7. Clean copy.
Definition to say back: "The articles are a, an and the. They are adjectives that point to nouns."
Rule: use a before a consonant sound and an before a vowel sound: a fox, an apple, an hour (the h is silent), a unicorn (it starts with a y sound).
Diagram: articles go on slants, just like adjectives. "The fox jumped." becomes fox | jumped, with The on a slant.
Write a or an: ___ ox · ___ almanac · ___ stove · ___ inventor · ___ hour · ___ kite · ___ eagle · ___ uniform.
Circle the articles and underline the other adjectives: The hungry fox saw a bunch of ripe grapes. An old almanac lay on the table.
Diagram: The hungry fox jumped. · An old ox walked. · A sour grape fell.
Dictation: "An ox and a cart went to the market. The farmer sold an old kettle."
Draft — retell The Fox and the Grapes, with a moral. 5–7 sentences. Check every a and an while drafting.
Checklist 1–7. Clean copy.
Definition to say back: "An adverb describes a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. It tells how, when, where, or to what extent."
Models: worked hard (how) · came yesterday (when) · ran outside (where) · very tired (to what extent). Many adverbs end in -ly: quickly, quietly, carefully. Not all do: fast, soon, here.
Diagram: adverbs hang on slants under the verb. "Amos whispered softly." becomes Amos | whispered, with softly on a slant under whispered.
Underline each adverb, then write which question it answers (how / when / where):
1. The country mouse ate slowly.
2. Ben arrived early.
3. The town mouse ran away.
4. The farmer worked carefully.
5. They walked home together.
Change the adjective to an adverb: quick → ___ · careful → ___ · quiet → ___ · happy → ___ (watch the y!).
Diagram: The mice ran quickly. · Ben wrote carefully. · The cat came suddenly.
Dictation: "The country mouse ate quietly. The cat came suddenly into the room."
Draft — retell The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse, with a moral. 5–7 sentences. Use at least one adverb that tells how the mice ran when the danger came.
Checklist 1–7. Clean copy.
Review: adjectives describe nouns; adverbs describe verbs.
Sort game: read words aloud (golden, greedily, foolish, quickly, every, soon) and the child says "adjective" or "adverb" and why.
Diagram together: "The foolish farmer quickly killed the goose." becomes farmer | killed, with The and foolish under farmer and quickly under killed. Goose waits until Term 4 (direct objects).
Label each underlined word ADJ or ADV: The golden egg shone brightly. The greedy man acted foolishly. Every morning the goose laid one egg.
Diagram: The greedy farmer waited impatiently. · The poor goose died sadly. · The shiny egg glowed brightly.
Dictation: "The farmer was very greedy. He foolishly killed the golden goose."
Draft — retell The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs, with a moral. 5–7 sentences.
Checklist 1–7. Clean copy.
If week 7 was a review week, skip this week's A and B (C and D still happen; the fable can move with them).
Definition to say back: "A singular noun names one. A plural noun names more than one."
Rules:
most nouns add -s: kite → kites
nouns ending in s, x, z, ch or sh add -es: box → boxes, church → churches
a consonant + y changes to -ies: colony → colonies
some nouns change completely: man → men, child → children, mouse → mice, goose → geese, foot → feet, ox → oxen
Coordinate with Spelling (03): if Spelling teaches these rules on a different week, follow Spelling's wording.
Write the plural: colony · wish · fox · city · mouse · ox · goose · tax · printer · child.
Fix the plural in each sentence: The two mouses ran away. · The farmer had three gooses. · Ben visited many citys.
Diagram: The cold winds blew. · The warm rays shone. · Many travelers stopped.
Dictation: "The North Wind and the Sun argued. Both wanted the traveler's cloak."
Draft — retell The North Wind and the Sun, with a moral. 5–7 sentences. Use at least two plural nouns.
Checklist 1–7. Clean copy.

weeks.title: Possessive nouns; review and term check

blocks.text: Definition to say back: "A possessive noun shows ownership."
Rules:
singular: add 's, as in the crow's cheese, Ben's kite
plural ending in s: add only ', as in the colonies' laws, the farmers' market
plural that doesn't end in s: add 's, as in the children's books, the mice's hole

Diagram: a possessive noun works like an adjective and goes on a slant. "Ben's kite flew." becomes kite | flew, with Ben's on a slant under kite. (Keep possessives in diagrams to names without an article, like Ben's or Amos's. "The crow's cheese" puts the with crow's, which comes in Grade 4.)
Review all five Term 2 definitions aloud.
Done independently, in one sitting, about 25 minutes. Answer key below.
Draft — retell The Fox and the Crow, with a moral. 5–7 sentences.
Checklist 1–7, then a clean copy. The parent marks the clean copy on the rubric below and files it in the portfolio.
Part 1 — Identify (10 items, one point each).
1–2. Circle the adjectives in "The proud crow held a large piece of cheese." (proud, large; articles don't count here)
3. Write a or an: ___ inventor.
4–5. Underline the adverbs in "The fox spoke sweetly and waited patiently."
6–7. Write the plurals: colony, ox.
8–9. Write the possessives: the cap belonging to Ben; the books belonging to the children.
10. Is quickly an adjective or an adverb?
Part 2 — Diagram (5 sentences: subject, verb and their describing words).
1. The clever fox smiled.
2. The proud crow sang loudly.
3. A small mouse squeaked.
4. Ben's kite rose high.
5. The cold wind blew fiercely.
Answer key.
Part 1: 1–2 proud, large · 3 an · 4–5 sweetly, patiently · 6 colonies · 7 oxen · 8 Ben's cap · 9 the children's books · 10 adverb.
Part 2:
1. fox | smiled; The, clever under fox.
2. crow | sang; The, proud under crow; loudly under sang.
3. mouse | squeaked; A, small under mouse.
4. kite | rose; Ben's under kite; high under rose.
5. wind | blew; The, cold under wind; fiercely under blew.
A diagram counts as correct when the baseline is right and every describing word hangs under the right word.
Mastery gate: 8 of 10 in Part 1 and 4 of 5 in Part 2. Below the gate, Term 3 week 13 becomes a review week, and week 17 (the Term 3 flex week) is skipped. Record the scores next to Term 1's.
Score each line 0, 1 or 2, for six points in all. Record the score, not a letter grade.

rows: Every event in order: the crow with cheese, the fox's flattery, the song, the cheese falling
Missing, or tells only what happened to the animals
A true lesson for people, said the child's own way
Many fragments, or no describing words
Complete sentences, with adjectives and an adverb used well

Slants are hard to draw neatly at first. A ruler helps, and so does lined paper turned sideways. The point is to show which word goes with which, not to be neat.
The moral sentence is the term's real work. Turning a story about animals into a truth about people is a first step toward abstract thought. Give it time; ask, don't tell.

head: Grammar
Personal pronouns; helping verbs; linking verbs with predicate nouns and adjectives; compound subjects and verbs; conjunctions
rows: Verb phrases on the baseline; predicate nouns and adjectives after a slanted line; compound subjects and verbs on forks
Progymnasmata stage 1, second operation: expand the fable with dialogue and description. 7–10 sentences, ending with the moral

From Literature, one week behind: The Milkmaid and Her Pail (wk 13), The Bundle of Sticks (wk 14), Belling the Cat (wk 15), The Dog and the Wolf (wk 16), The Wolf and the Lamb (wk 17), The Frogs Who Desired a King (wk 18)
Drawn from Literature Term 3: Washington, Paul Revere, Sam the Minuteman

glance.text: If the child was below the Term 2 gate. Week 13 becomes a review week: repeat the missed Term 2 lessons (A) and redo the missed parts of the check (B). Composition in week 13 goes ahead as written. Then teach weeks 13–16 in weeks 14–17, skip week 17's flex lesson, and do week 18 as written.

blocks.text: Verb phrases. Helping verb and main verb go on the baseline together, in the verb's place: Revere | was riding.
Linking verbs. After the verb, draw a short line slanting back toward the subject, and write the predicate noun or adjective after it. The slant shows that the word points back to the subject.
Washington | was \ general
"Washington was a general." General renames Washington. "The night was dark." Dark describes night. Both use the slanted line.
Compound subjects and verbs split into a fork, with the conjunction written on a dotted line between the prongs.
Sam \
and ---- | marched
father /
"Sam and his father marched." Two subjects share one verb. A compound verb forks on the right side in the same way.
1. Every sentence starts with a capital letter.
2. Every sentence ends with the right mark (. ? !).
3. Every sentence is complete.
4. Names of people and places have capital letters.
5. All the fable's events are there, in order.
6. The last sentence states the moral in your own words.
7. New: At least two characters speak, with their words inside quotation marks.
8. New: At least one sentence that helps us see the place or a character.
Spelling is circled and corrected, not scored. From this term, the child also checks: have I used I and me correctly? (week 13).
Teach this once, in week 13 task C, before the first draft.
What a character says goes inside quotation marks: "I'll have a fine new dress," said the milkmaid.
The comma or end mark goes inside the closing quotation mark.
Start a new line each time a different character speaks.
Said is fine, and so are asked, whispered, cried, boasted. Don't overdo it.
To expand a fable is to tell the same story at greater length without changing what happens. The student adds:
dialogue: what the characters might have said
description: what the place, the weather or a character looked like
thoughts and feelings: what a character was thinking

The student must not add new events or change the ending. That's the whole discipline of the exercise: the plot stays fixed and the telling grows. Expanding is the opposite of Term 4's condensing, and doing both teaches the child that the same story can be told at any length.
Definition to say back: "A pronoun takes the place of a noun."
Subject pronouns (they can be the subject): I, you, he, she, it, we, they.
Object pronouns (they come after the verb or after words like to and with): me, you, him, her, it, us, them.
The test: take out the other person. "Sam and me ran"? Take out Sam: "me ran". No. It's "Sam and I ran."
Diagram: a subject pronoun sits on the baseline like a noun: He | rode.
Replace the underlined noun with a pronoun: Paul Revere rode all night. Washington thanked the soldiers. Sam's mother waved goodbye.
Choose the right pronoun: (I / me) watched the redcoats. · The captain gave (we / us) muskets. · Sam and (he / him) waited on the green. · Father walked with Sam and (I / me).
Diagram: He rode. · They waited. · We marched bravely.
Dictation: "Sam and I heard the bell. We ran to the green."

Draft — expand The Milkmaid and Her Pail. 7–10 sentences. Teach "How to write dialogue" and "What 'expand' means" first. Let the milkmaid say her daydream aloud, describe the pail and the road, and end with the moral.
Checklist 1–8, plus the I/me check. Clean copy.
Definition to say back: "A helping verb comes before the main verb and helps it show time or meaning. Together they make a verb phrase."
List to chant (and add to Memory Work): is, am, are, was, were, be, being, been · has, have, had · do, does, did · will, would, shall, should, can, could, may, might, must.
Models: Revere was riding · the soldiers had waited · Washington will lead.
Diagram: the whole verb phrase goes on the baseline in the verb's place: soldiers | had waited.
Underline the helping verb once and the main verb twice:
1. The bells were ringing.
2. Washington had crossed the river.
3. The redcoats are coming.
4. Sam could hear the drums.
5. The colonists will fight.
Diagram: The bells were ringing. · The brothers had argued. · The old father was speaking.
Dictation: "The sons were quarreling again. Their father had called them together."
Draft — expand The Bundle of Sticks. 7–10 sentences. Let the father speak to his sons, and let at least one son answer.
Checklist 1–8. Clean copy.
Definition to say back: "A linking verb joins the subject to a word that renames it or describes it."
Common linking verbs: forms of be (is, am, are, was, were), and seem, become, feel, look, appear.
Predicate noun renames the subject: "Washington was a surveyor." Predicate adjective describes the subject: "The plan was foolish."
The test: can you swap in an equal sign? Washington = surveyor. If so, it's linking.
Diagram: subject | verb, then a slanted line back toward the subject, then the predicate word.
Label each sentence: action verb or linking verb:
1. The old mouse spoke up.
2. The plan seemed clever.
3. The cat was dangerous.
4. Revere was a silversmith.
5. The mice ran away.
Circle the predicate noun or adjective in the linking sentences.
Diagram: The plan was foolish. · Revere was a silversmith. · The cat seemed sleepy.
Dictation: "The young mouse was very proud. His plan seemed simple."
7–10 sentences. Hold a mouse council: let three different mice speak, including the old mouse with the hard question.
Checklist 1–8. Clean copy.
Definition to say back: "A conjunction joins words or groups of words. The most common are and, but and or."
Compound subject: two subjects share one verb: "The dog and the wolf talked."
Compound verb: one subject does two things: "The wolf looked and listened."
Diagram: a fork, with the conjunction on a dotted line between the prongs. Each prong carries its own describing words.
Underline the compound subject or compound verb, and circle the conjunction:
1. Washington and his men crossed the river.
2. The soldiers shivered and waited.
3. Sam or his father will go.
4. The dog barked but stayed.
Combine each pair into one sentence: The dog was fed. The dog was chained. · Revere rode. Dawes rode.
Diagram: The dog and the wolf talked. · The wolf looked and listened. · Sam and his father marched.
Dictation: "The dog and the wolf met in the woods. The wolf listened and wondered."
Draft — expand The Dog and the Wolf. 7–10 sentences. Most of this fable is conversation, so let it be. Use at least one compound subject or verb.
Checklist 1–8. Clean copy.
Review all four Term 3 lessons with one sentence each, said back and diagrammed together.

Revise a sentence aloud: start with "The wolf was hungry." Make it compound ("The wolf was hungry and angry"). Add a helping verb in a new sentence ("He was looking for a reason"). Then replace "the wolf" with a pronoun.
Name the part of speech of each underlined word: He (pronoun) was (linking verb) cruel. The lamb and (conjunction) the wolf were drinking (verb phrase).
Diagram: The wolf was cruel. · The lamb and the wolf were drinking. · She answered politely.
Dictation: "The lamb was drinking at the stream. The wolf was looking for a quarrel."
Draft — expand The Wolf and the Lamb. 7–10 sentences. The wolf makes excuses; the lamb answers each one. Let the dialogue carry the story.
Checklist 1–8. Clean copy.
If week 13 was a review week, skip this week's A and B (C and D still happen).

Part 1 — Identify (10 items, one point each).
1–2. Choose the right pronoun: (1) "(Him / He) rode to Lexington." (2) "The captain called Sam and (I / me)."
3–4. Underline the verb phrase: (3) "The redcoats were marching." (4) "Washington had planned the attack."
5. Is seemed in "The night seemed endless" an action verb or a linking verb?
6. In the same sentence, what is endless: a predicate noun or a predicate adjective?
7. In "Revere was a silversmith," what is silversmith?
8–9. Underline the compound subject in "Sam and his father waited," and the compound verb in "The soldiers shivered and prayed."
10. Name the conjunction in "Sam or his father will go."
Part 2 — Diagram (5 sentences).
1. They marched bravely.
2. The bells were ringing.
3. The winter was cruel.
4. Washington was a leader.
5. Sam and his father waited.
Answer key.
Part 1: 1 He · 2 me · 3 were marching · 4 had planned · 5 linking · 6 predicate adjective · 7 predicate noun · 8 Sam and his father · 9 shivered and prayed · 10 or.
Part 2:
1. They | marched; bravely under marched.
2. bells | were ringing; The under bells.
3. winter | was \ cruel; The under winter.
4. Washington | was \ leader; a under leader.
5. Fork: Sam and father (with his under father), and on the dotted line, then | waited.
Mastery gate: 8 of 10 in Part 1 and 4 of 5 in Part 2. Below the gate, Term 4 week 19 becomes a review week. Record the scores next to Terms 1–2.
Score each line 0, 1 or 2, for six points in all. Record the score, not a letter grade.

rows: Every event kept in order: the log, the frogs' scorn, the stork; nothing invented
One of the two, or punctuation slips
Frogs speak in correct quotation marks, and the log or stork is clearly described
A few slips, or a vague moral
Complete sentences and a clear moral in the child's own words

blocks.text: 4 or more is on track. Below 4, Term 4 keeps paragraph work short (see the Term 4 manual).

Expanding tempts children to invent. If the milkmaid suddenly buys a horse and rides to London, the child has written a new story, not expanded a fable. Praise the energy, and ask them to keep the plot and add words instead.
Dialogue punctuation will take the whole term. Correct it in revision, not during the draft.
Latin I (09) will meet pronouns and to be (sum, es, est) this year as well. If Latin reaches them first, use its vocabulary of "subject" and "linking verb" to connect the two.

terms.title: Grammar: prepositions, direct objects, the paragraph · Composition: Condense the fable

head: Grammar
Prepositions and prepositional phrases; phrases that work as adjectives or adverbs; direct objects; the paragraph
rows: Prepositional phrases on a slant-and-line under the word they describe; direct objects on the baseline after a short upright line
Progymnasmata stage 1, third operation: condense the fable, first to three sentences, then to one, then into a paragraph with a topic sentence

From Literature, one week behind: The Lark and Her Young Ones (wk 19), The Belly and the Members (wk 20), The Miller, His Son, and the Donkey (wk 21), The Two Travelers and the Bear (wk 22), The Oak and the Reeds (wk 23), The Fox Without a Tail (wk 24)
Drawn from Literature Term 4: John Hancock, the Constitutional Convention, Toliver's Secret

glance.text: If the child was below the Term 3 gate. Week 19 becomes a review week: repeat the missed Term 3 lessons (A) and redo the missed parts of the check (B). Composition in week 19 goes ahead as written. Then teach weeks 19–22 in weeks 20–23, skip week 23's flex lesson, and do week 24 as written.
If the child scored below 4 on the Term 3 fable rubric, keep weeks 22–24 to a short paragraph: a topic sentence plus three sentences.
Order each week. A before B. C before D, in different sittings, with D at least a day later. The two pairs can be done in any order.
Link to Literature. Literature offers an early paragraph in week 24 and holds its paragraph gate in week 25. This term's paragraph lessons (weeks 22–24) come just before both on purpose.

blocks.text: Prepositional phrases hang below the word they describe. Draw a slanted line for the preposition and a flat line for its object, like a hockey stick. Describing words for the object hang below the flat line.
"Ellen walked through the city." The phrase tells where she walked, so it hangs under walked:
Ellen | walked
\through
city
\the
Direct objects sit on the baseline after the verb, separated by a short upright line that does not cross the baseline.
Hancock | signed | Declaration
"Hancock signed the Declaration." The hangs under Declaration, as before.
1. Every sentence starts with a capital letter.
2. Every sentence ends with the right mark.
3. Every sentence is complete.
4. Names of people and places have capital letters.
5. Changed: The main events are all there, in order, and nothing important is lost.
6. The moral is stated in your own words.
7. New: Every word earns its place. Could a word or sentence be cut without losing anything?
8. New from week 22: The paragraph starts with a topic sentence, and every sentence stays on it.
Spelling is circled and corrected, not scored.

To condense a fable is to tell the same story in fewer words without losing what matters. It's the opposite of Term 3's expanding. The student keeps the main events and the point, and cuts description, dialogue and anything that could go. Doing both, expanding and condensing, teaches that the writer controls the length, and the story stays the same.
The three-sentence form: one sentence each for the beginning, the middle and the end.
The one-sentence form: the whole fable, with its point, in one sentence. It's harder than it looks, and it's the seed of every summary and thesis the student will ever write.
Teach this in week 22 task A.
A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea.
The topic sentence comes first and names the main idea.
Supporting sentences tell more about it, in order.
Every sentence must stay on the topic. A sentence that wanders belongs somewhere else.
The first line is indented: start a thumb's width in from the margin.

For a condensed fable, the topic sentence names what the fable is about and its point. For example: "In The Two Travelers and the Bear, a man learns who his real friend is." Then 3–5 sentences of the story, and a final sentence with the moral.
Definition to say back: "A preposition shows how a noun or pronoun is related to another word in the sentence."

List to chant (add to Memory Work): about, above, across, after, against, along, among, around, at, before, behind, below, beneath, beside, between, beyond, by, down, during, for, from, in, inside, into, near, of, off, on, out, over, past, since, through, to, toward, under, until, up, upon, with, within, without.
Prepositional phrase: a preposition plus its object and any words describing it: through the city, under the British flag, with a loaf.
Diagram: the hockey-stick shape, hanging under the word it describes.
Put parentheses around each prepositional phrase and underline the preposition:
1. Ellen walked through the city.
2. The loaf was under her arm.
3. The delegates met in Philadelphia.
4. Hancock wrote with a large pen.
5. The lark built a nest in the field.
Diagram: Ellen walked through the city. · The lark lived in a field. · The soldiers marched past the house.
Dictation: "The lark built her nest in a field of wheat. Her young birds lived among the stalks."

Draft — condense The Lark and Her Young Ones to three sentences. One sentence for the beginning, one for the middle, one for the end. Read "What 'condense' means" together first. Add the moral as a fourth sentence.
Checklist 1–7. Clean copy.

weeks.title: Prepositional phrases as adjectives and adverbs

blocks.text: Definition to say back: "A prepositional phrase can work like an adjective, describing a noun, or like an adverb, describing a verb."
Models:
"The man in the blue coat signed." The phrase tells which man, so it's adjectival and hangs under man.
"He signed with a flourish." The phrase tells how he signed, so it's adverbial and hangs under signed.
The test: ask what the phrase describes. Which one? points to a noun. How, when, where? point to a verb.
Write ADJ or ADV for each phrase, and draw an arrow to the word it describes:
1. The hands of the body refused.
2. The members worked without rest.
3. The belly in the middle waited.
4. The delegates argued during the summer.
Diagram: The hands of the body rebelled. · The delegates argued during the summer. · The man in the blue coat signed.
Dictation: "The hands and feet argued with the belly. The parts of the body grew weak."
Draft — condense The Belly and the Members to three sentences, then to one. Write the three-sentence version first. Below it, write the whole fable in a single sentence that includes its point.
Checklist 1–7. Clean copy of both versions.
Definition to say back: "A direct object receives the action of the verb. It answers whom? or what? after an action verb."
How to find it: find the verb, then the subject, then ask "subject verb what?" "Ellen carried what?" The loaf. Loaf is the direct object.
Not every sentence has one. Linking verbs never do: "Ellen was brave" has a predicate adjective, not a direct object.
Diagram: after the verb on the baseline, a short upright line that stops at the baseline, then the direct object.
Underline the verb and circle the direct object. Write "none" if there isn't one:
1. Ellen carried the loaf.
2. The miller sold his donkey.
3. The son rode the donkey.
4. The people laughed.
5. The delegates wrote a constitution.
6. The plan was good.
Diagram: Ellen carried the loaf. · The miller sold the donkey. · The delegates wrote a constitution.
Dictation: "The miller and his son led their donkey to market. People mocked them on the road."

Draft — condense The Miller, His Son, and the Donkey. This fable has many events (each passerby's advice), which makes condensing harder. Write three sentences, then one. Decide which events can be grouped together.
Checklist 1–7. Clean copy of both versions.
Teach "What a paragraph is" (above).
Definitions to say back: "A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea. The topic sentence names the main idea."
Model: read this paragraph aloud and find the topic sentence:

In The Two Travelers and the Bear, a man learns who his real friend is. Two friends are walking through a forest when a bear appears. One climbs a tree and leaves the other behind. The second man lies still, and the bear sniffs him and goes away. He tells his friend that the bear whispered, "Never travel with a friend who deserts you."
Find the stray: read the model again with an extra sentence added, "Bears like to eat honey." The child finds the sentence that wanders off the topic.
Diagram (direct objects and phrases together): The friend climbed a tree. · The bear sniffed the man. · The traveler lay on the ground.
Topic sentences: write a topic sentence for a paragraph about (1) Ellen's journey, (2) the Constitutional Convention, (3) your own favorite fable.
Dictation: "One traveler climbed a tree. The other lay still on the ground."
Draft — The Two Travelers and the Bear as a paragraph. Topic sentence, 3–5 sentences of the story, then the moral. Don't copy the model; use your own words.
Checklist 1–8. Clean copy, indented.
Diagram one sentence that uses everything this year so far: "The tall oak stood proudly beside the river." oak | stood; The, tall under oak; proudly under stood; beside the river hangs under stood.
Then one with a direct object: "The wind bent the reeds." wind | bent | reeds.

Name the job of each word in italics (answers in brackets): The wind broke [verb] the oak [direct object]. The reeds bent in the storm [prepositional phrase working as an adverb]. The oak was [linking verb] proud [predicate adjective].
Diagram: The storm broke the oak. · The reeds bent low in the wind. · The proud oak fell into the river.
Dictation: "The oak stood tall and proud. The reeds bent low in the wind."
Draft — The Oak and the Reeds as a paragraph. Topic sentence, 3–5 sentences, moral.
Checklist 1–8. Clean copy.
If week 19 was a review week, skip this week's A and B (C and D still happen).

weeks.title: Review, term check and marked paragraph

blocks.text: The child says the Term 4 definitions back (preposition, prepositional phrase, direct object, paragraph, topic sentence), chants the preposition list, and diagrams one sentence of each kind with you.
Done independently, in one sitting, about 25 minutes. Answer key below.
Draft — The Fox Without a Tail as a paragraph. Topic sentence, 3–5 sentences, moral.
Checklist 1–8, then a clean copy. The parent marks the clean copy on the rubric below and files it in the portfolio. This paragraph is also good evidence for Literature's paragraph gate in week 25.
Part 1 — Identify (10 items, one point each).
1–2. Put parentheses around the prepositional phrases in "The fox walked into the meeting with a strange plan."
3. In item 1–2, what is the object of the preposition into?
4. Is of the body in "The hands of the body rebelled" working as an adjective or an adverb?
5–6. Circle the direct object: (5) "Hancock signed the Declaration." (6) "The fox lost his tail."
7. Does "Ellen was brave" have a direct object? (yes / no)
8. Write a preposition that means the opposite of above.
9. What is the sentence that names a paragraph's main idea called?

10. In the paragraph below, which sentence wanders off the topic? (1) The miller tried to please everyone. (2) First he walked beside the donkey. (3) Donkeys are related to horses. (4) Then he let his son ride.
Part 2 — Diagram (5 sentences).
1. The fox lost his tail.
2. Ellen walked through the snow.
3. The delegates met in Philadelphia.
4. The man in the coat signed the paper.
5. The wind bent the reeds.
Answer key.
Part 1: 1–2 (into the meeting), (with a strange plan) · 3 meeting · 4 adjective (tells which hands) · 5 Declaration · 6 tail · 7 no · 8 below, under or beneath · 9 the topic sentence · 10 sentence 3.
Part 2:
1. fox | lost | tail; The under fox; his under tail.
2. Ellen | walked; through / snow hangs under walked, with the under snow.
3. delegates | met; The under delegates; in / Philadelphia hangs under met.
4. man | signed | paper; The under man, and in / coat (with the) also hangs under man; the under paper.
5. wind | bent | reeds; The under wind; the under reeds.
Mastery gate: 8 of 10 in Part 1 and 4 of 5 in Part 2. Below the gate, Term 5 week 25 becomes a review week. Record the scores next to Terms 1–3.
Score each line 0, 1 or 2, for six points in all. Record the score, not a letter grade.

The fox loses his tail, tries to persuade the others, and is found out, with nothing extra
Topic sentence present, but a sentence strays
Indented; topic sentence names the fable and its point; every sentence stays on it
A few slips, or a vague moral
Complete sentences and a clear moral in the child's own words

Condensing feels like losing to some children. After a term of being praised for adding, cutting can seem wrong. Tell them plainly: knowing what to leave out is a writer's skill, and the best writers do both.
The one-sentence summary is hard. Accept a long sentence at first. By week 21 aim for one under 30 words.
Diagram sizes grow this term. Use a whole page for each diagram and plenty of space under the baseline.

head: Grammar
Simple verb tenses (past, present, future); indirect objects; compound sentences; interjections. All eight parts of speech are complete by week 30.
rows: Indirect objects under the verb; compound sentences on two baselines joined by a dotted step; interjections on a line of their own
Progymnasmata stage 1, fourth operation: change the point of view. Retell the fable as one of its characters, in the first person, as a paragraph

From Literature, one week behind: The Ass in the Lion's Skin (wk 25), The Gnat and the Bull (wk 26), The Farmer and His Sons (wk 27), The Mountain in Labor (wk 28), The Fox and the Cat (wk 29), The Crab and Its Mother (wk 30)
Drawn from Literature Term 5: the tall tales, Johnny Appleseed, Lewis and Clark

glance.text: If the child was below the Term 4 gate. Week 25 becomes a review week: repeat the missed Term 4 lessons (A) and redo the missed parts of the check (B). Composition in week 25 goes ahead as written. Then teach weeks 25–28 in weeks 26–29, skip week 29's flex lesson, and do week 30 as written.

Link to Literature's paragraph gate (week 25). A child who passes writes this term's retellings as paragraphs. A child who hasn't passed yet writes 5–7 sentences in the first person, without the paragraph requirement, and switches to paragraphs once the gate is passed (Literature retries it in week 28).

blocks.text: Indirect objects hang under the verb like a prepositional phrase with an empty slant, because "to" or "for" is understood but not written.
Johnny | gave | seeds
\ (empty)
settlers
"Johnny gave the settlers seeds." He gave seeds (direct object) to the settlers (indirect object). The hangs under settlers.
Compound sentences get two full baselines, one above the other, joined at the verbs by a dotted line with a step. The conjunction sits on the step.
Lewis | led
: and
Clark | drew | maps
"Lewis led, and Clark drew maps."
Interjections sit on a short line of their own, above and to the left of the baseline, unconnected to the rest.
1. Every sentence starts with a capital letter.
2. Every sentence ends with the right mark.
3. Every sentence is complete.
4. Names of people and places have capital letters.
5. All the main events are there, in order.
6. The moral is stated in your own words.
7. The paragraph has a topic sentence, and every sentence stays on it. (Paragraph writers.)
8. New: The story is told by one character, using I and me, the whole way through.
9. New: The verbs stay in the past tense the whole way through.
Spelling is circled and corrected, not scored.

reference.title: What "change the point of view" means

blocks.text: Teach this in week 25 task C, before the first draft.
Every fable has a narrator who stands outside the story: "A donkey found a lion's skin…"
To change the point of view, the student steps inside and becomes one of the characters: "I found a lion's skin lying in the grass…"
The events stay exactly the same. Only who's telling them changes.
The new narrator can tell only what they could see, hear and think. The ass doesn't know what the fox is thinking unless the fox says it.
The moral comes at the end, as the character's own lesson: "I learned that…"

This is the last of the four stage-1 operations. A narrator who stays in one point of view, like a writer who stays in one tense, is learning control. Choosing a minor character, such as the bull rather than the gnat, is often the most interesting version.
Link to Literature. In Term 1 week 4 the child retold the Mayflower voyage as a child on board. This is the same move, now done every week and on purpose.
Definition to say back: "Tense shows the time of the action. Past tense tells what already happened, present tense what is happening now, and future tense what will happen."
Models:
walk: walked (past) · walk / walks (present) · will walk (future)
Irregular verbs change their spelling: go, went · see, saw · find, found · run, ran · give, gave · come, came · take, took · say, said

The narrator's rule: stories are usually told in the past tense, and they stay there. Mixing tenses in a story ("I walked to the river and I see a bear") is the most common slip in first-person writing.
Diagram: the verb's tense doesn't change the diagram; will walk sits on the baseline as a verb phrase, like Term 3's helping verbs.
Write all three tenses: plant · carry · find · go · see.
Fix the tense so the whole passage is past: "Johnny walked west. He carries a sack of seeds. He plants them by the rivers. Later, trees grew there."
Diagram: Johnny planted seeds. · The settlers will build cabins. · Pecos Bill rode a cyclone.
Dictation: "Johnny Appleseed walked across the land. He planted apple seeds everywhere."
Draft — The Ass in the Lion's Skin, told by the ass. Read "What 'change the point of view' means" together first. Start with "I…". Keep every verb in the past tense.
Checklist 1–9. Clean copy.
Definition to say back: "An indirect object tells to whom or for whom the action is done. It comes between the verb and the direct object."

How to find it: first find the direct object. Then ask "to whom?" or "for whom?". "Sacagawea showed the captains the trail." Showed what? Trail (direct object). Showed it to whom? Captains (indirect object).
The test: you can move it into a to or for phrase: "showed the trail to the captains." If you can, it's an indirect object.
No direct object, no indirect object.
Circle the direct object and underline the indirect object:
1. Sacagawea showed the captains the trail.
2. The Mandan gave the explorers corn.
3. Johnny handed the children apples.
4. Clark drew Jefferson a map.
Rewrite each with to or for instead: sentences 1 and 3.
Diagram: The Mandan gave the explorers corn. · Johnny handed the children apples. · The bull gave the gnat no answer.
Dictation: "The gnat told the bull his name. The bull paid him no attention."
Draft — The Gnat and the Bull, told by the bull. The bull barely noticed the gnat. Let that show. The child can make the bull's voice slow and puzzled.
Checklist 1–9. Clean copy.
Definition to say back: "A compound sentence is two complete sentences joined by a comma and a conjunction."
Joining words: and (adds), but (contrasts), or (gives a choice).
The comma goes before the conjunction: "The sons dug the field, but they found no gold."
Not every and makes a compound sentence. "The sons dug and planted" is one sentence with a compound verb (Term 3). The test: can each side stand alone with its own subject and verb?
Diagram: two baselines, joined by a dotted step with the conjunction on it.
Write C for compound sentence or S for simple sentence with a compound part:
1. The farmer was dying, and his sons gathered round.
2. The sons dug and searched.
3. They found no treasure, but the harvest was rich.
4. Lewis and Clark traveled west.
Join each pair into a compound sentence with the right comma and conjunction: The river was wide. The boats crossed it safely. · We can walk. We can ride.
Diagram: The sons dug, and the vines grew. · The river was deep, but the boats crossed. · Clark drew maps, and Lewis wrote notes.
Dictation: "The sons dug the whole field, but they found no gold. The vines grew strong, and the harvest was large."
Draft — The Farmer and His Sons, told by one of the sons. Use at least one compound sentence. The son might not understand his father's words until the end.
Checklist 1–9. Clean copy.

weeks.title: Interjections; all eight parts of speech

blocks.text: Definition to say back: "An interjection is a word that shows strong feeling or surprise. It is not connected to the rest of the sentence."
Models: Wow! Oh no! Hurrah! Alas, the boat sank. Well, we'll try again. A strong interjection takes an exclamation mark; a mild one takes a comma.
The eight parts of speech are now complete. Chant them together and add the chant to Memory Work: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection.
Diagram: the interjection on its own short line, above and to the left.
Underline the interjection and add the right punctuation: Hurrah we reached the ocean · Oh the mountain is shaking · Well that was a small mouse.
Name the part of speech of every word: "Wow, the huge mountain shook loudly!"
(Wow, interjection · the, adjective · huge, adjective · mountain, noun · shook, verb · loudly, adverb)
Diagram: Hurrah! The explorers reached the ocean. · Oh, the mountain shook. · Alas, the mouse ran away.
Dictation: "Oh, the mountain shook and roared! Out came a tiny mouse."
Draft — The Mountain in Labor, told by a villager watching. A villager is a new character, not in the fable, but someone who could have been there. Use one interjection.
Checklist 1–9. Clean copy.
Diagram together, one at a time:
"The cat climbed a tree." Direct object.
"The fox showed the cat his tricks." Indirect object.
"The dogs came, and the fox ran." Compound sentence.
Tense check: read a paragraph from one of the term's drafts aloud and listen for any slip out of the past tense.
Identify all the parts of the sentence: "The clever fox told the cat a hundred tricks, but the cat knew only one."
Diagram: The fox told the cat his tricks. · The hounds came, and the cat climbed. · Alas! The fox waited too long.
Dictation: "The fox had a hundred tricks, but the cat had only one. The cat's trick saved her life."
Draft — The Fox and the Cat, told by the cat.
Checklist 1–9. Clean copy.
If week 25 was a review week, skip this week's A and B (C and D still happen).

weeks.title: Review, term check and marked retelling

blocks.text: The child says the Term 5 definitions back, chants the eight parts of speech, and diagrams one sentence of each Term 5 kind with you.
Done independently, in one sitting, about 25 minutes. Answer key below.
Draft — The Crab and Its Mother, told by the young crab.
Checklist 1–9, then a clean copy. The parent marks the clean copy on the rubric below and files it in the portfolio.

Note on Literature's tall tale (week 30). Literature asks the child to write an original tall tale this same week. It's an invented story, not a retelling, so it isn't marked here, but the tense and point-of-view habits from this term apply. Expect it to be the year's liveliest piece of writing.
Part 1 — Identify (10 items, one point each).
1–3. Write the past tense: (1) plant (2) go (3) find.
4. What tense is "will cross"?
5. Underline the indirect object: "Clark gave the chief a medal."
6. Circle the direct object in the same sentence.
7. Is this a compound sentence? "The sons dug and planted the field." (yes / no)
8. Add the missing comma: "The river was wide but the boats crossed."
9. Underline the interjection: "Hurrah, we found the ocean!"
10. List the eight parts of speech. (Score one point for all eight; no partial credit.)
Part 2 — Diagram (5 sentences).
1. Johnny planted trees.
2. The chief gave Clark horses.
3. The sons dug, and the vines grew.
4. Wow! The bull laughed.
5. The cat will climb the tree.
Answer key.

Part 1: 1 planted · 2 went · 3 found · 4 future · 5 chief · 6 medal · 7 no (one subject, compound verb) · 8 "wide, but" · 9 Hurrah · 10 noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection.
Part 2:
1. Johnny | planted | trees.
2. chief | gave | horses; The under chief; Clark on the empty-slant indirect object line under gave.
3. Two baselines: sons | dug (with The), and vines | grew (with the), joined by a dotted step labeled and.
4. Wow on its own line; bull | laughed, with The under bull.
5. cat | will climb | tree; The under cat; the under tree.
Mastery gate: 8 of 10 in Part 1 and 4 of 5 in Part 2. Below the gate, Term 6 week 31 becomes a review week. Record the scores next to Terms 1–4.
Score each line 0, 1 or 2, for six points in all. Record the score, not a letter grade.

rows: Events changed, or the narrator keeps slipping out
Events kept; one or two slips in point of view
The mother's scolding, her walk, and the lesson all kept, told only by the young crab, with I throughout
Past tense all the way through
No paragraph form (if required), or no moral
A wandering sentence, or a vague moral
Topic sentence, stays on topic, and ends with the crab's own lesson

blocks.text: 4 or more is on track.
Point-of-view slips are normal. Halfway through, the child often slides back into "the ass did…". Don't correct it in the draft; point it out in revision, using checklist line 8.
The minor character is often the best narrator. The bull, a villager, a son: these voices force the child to imagine more.
The eight parts of speech are the year's grammar milestone. Celebrate it in week 28. Term 6 reviews them, and Grade 4 builds on them.
Check the Term 4 gate and rubric results, and Literature's week 25 paragraph gate result
Print the Term 5 revision checklist (now nine lines) and "What 'change the point of view' means"
Add the irregular past-tense list and the eight parts of speech to the Memory Work queue
Week 30: give the term check, mark the retelling, record both scores and file the clean copy in the portfolio

terms.mastery: Mastery gate: 8 of 10 in Part 1 and 4 of 5 in Part 2. Below the gate, Term 6 week 31 becomes a review week. Record the scores next to Terms 1–4.

terms.title: Grammar: year review and mastery check · Composition: One fable, the full treatment

head: Grammar
Review of the whole year by topic: nouns and pronouns; verbs; modifiers and phrases; sentence parts; sentence kinds. Year-end mastery check in week 36
rows: Every pattern from the year, ending with sentences that combine several
Full treatment: the child chooses one fable and takes it through all four stage-1 operations, one per week (retell, expand, condense, change point of view), then writes and tells a final version
The child's pick from the 30 fables of Terms 1–5. It must be one they already know well. Literature's Term 6 fables are read and discussed only, not written
Drawn from Literature Term 6: Lincoln and the child's chosen independent book, plus favorite sentences from the year

glance.text: If the child was below the Term 5 gate. Week 31 becomes a review week for the missed Term 5 lessons, and week 35's flex lesson is skipped. Composition goes ahead as written.
Order each week. A before B. C before D, in different sittings, with D at least a day later. The two pairs can be done in any order.

blocks.text: All year each operation was practiced on a different fable. Doing all four on the same fable shows the child what the operations are for: one story can be told long or short, from outside or inside, and stay itself. The final version in week 36, chosen and polished by the child, is their first piece of composition that's truly their own. It's the top of stage 1 and the bridge to stage 2 (narrative) in Grade 4.

Help the child choose in week 31. A good choice has two or three characters, a clear turn in the middle and a moral the child can say easily. The Lion and the Mouse, The Fox and the Crow, The North Wind and the Sun and The Dog and the Wolf all work well.
Use the checklist line for each week's operation, plus lines 1–4 every week:
1. Every sentence starts with a capital letter.
2. Every sentence ends with the right mark.
3. Every sentence is complete.
4. Names and proper nouns have capitals.
Retell (wk 31): every event in order; moral in your own words.
Expand (wk 32): same events; dialogue in quotation marks; at least one sentence that helps us see.
Condense (wk 33): three sentences, then one; nothing important lost.
Paragraph (wk 34): topic sentence; every sentence on topic; indented.
Point of view (wk 35): one narrator, I throughout; past tense throughout.
Final version (wk 36): the child's own checklist (see week 36).
Say back: noun; common and proper; singular and plural; possessive; pronoun; subject and object pronouns.
Quick drill: the parent says a word (Lincoln, cabin, children, Abe's, him), and the child names what kind it is.
Diagram together: "Young Abe read books." · "He borrowed them."
Underline every noun and circle every pronoun: "Abe and his sister walked to the little school, but they did not stay long."
Plurals and possessives: write the plural of child, city, ox; write the axe belonging to Abe and the books belonging to the neighbors.
Choose: (He / Him) and (I / me) read by the fire.
Diagram: Abe read books. · They walked home. · Lincoln's mother taught him.
Dictation: "Abe borrowed every book in the county. He read them by firelight."
Retell your chosen fable faithfully, ending with the moral in your own words. 5–7 sentences.
Lines 1–4 plus the retell line. Clean copy. Keep every clean copy this term in one folder.
Say back: action verb; helping verb (chant the list); linking verb; tense.
Sort game: split, was, will run, seemed, has read, became, laughed. The child sorts them into action, linking and verb phrase.
Diagram together: "Abe was a rail-splitter." · "He had split many rails."
Label each verb A (action), L (linking) or VP (verb phrase with a helper):
1. Abe split rails.
2. Abe was honest.
3. The flatboat was floating down the river.
4. Lincoln became president.
Write the past tense: see, go, take, give, run, buy.
Diagram: Abe split rails. · Lincoln became president. · The boat was floating.
Dictation: "Abe was tall and strong. He had split thousands of rails."
Tell the same fable at greater length, with dialogue and description. 8–12 sentences. Keep every event.
Lines 1–4 plus the expand line. Clean copy.
Say back: adjective; article; adverb; preposition; prepositional phrase.
What does it describe? For each modifier, the child points to the word it describes: "The tall man walked slowly down the dusty road."
Diagram together: "The tall man walked slowly down the road."
Label each word or phrase in bold ADJ, ADV or PREP PHRASE: "A kind storekeeper walked quickly through the night with two pennies."
(A, ADJ · kind, ADJ · quickly, ADV · through the night, PREP PHRASE working as an adverb · two, ADJ)
Diagram: The honest storekeeper returned the pennies. · Abe walked through the snow. · A boy from Kentucky became a great man.
Dictation: "Abe walked six miles in the dark. He returned the pennies to the woman."
Tell the same fable in three sentences, then in one.
Lines 1–4 plus the condense line. Clean copy of both.
Say back: subject; predicate; direct object; indirect object; predicate noun; predicate adjective.
The question chain: for any sentence, ask in order: What's the verb? Who or what does it? Verb what? To or for whom? Is the verb linking? What does it link to?
Diagram together: "Lincoln gave the nation a promise." · "The war was long."
Mark S, V, DO, IO, PN or PA above each main word:
1. Lincoln gave the soldiers hope.
2. The war was terrible.
3. Lincoln was a lawyer.
4. The people elected Lincoln.
Diagram: Lincoln gave the soldiers hope. · Lincoln was a lawyer. · The people elected him.
Dictation: "The people chose Lincoln. He gave the country his whole strength."
Write the condensed fable as a paragraph: topic sentence, 3–5 sentences, moral.
Lines 1–4 plus the paragraph line. Clean copy.

weeks.title: Kinds of sentences; putting it all together (flex week)

blocks.text: Say back: the four kinds of sentences; conjunction; compound sentence; interjection; and the eight parts of speech chant.

Diagram together: "The North fought, and the South fought." · "Alas! The war lasted four years." · "Did Lincoln free the slaves?" (Questions diagram like statements: put the words in statement order first, "Lincoln did free slaves.")
Label each sentence: declarative, interrogative, imperative or exclamatory; and simple or compound.
1. Read the Gettysburg Address.
2. Lincoln spoke briefly, but the people remembered.
3. What a great speech it was!
4. Where was Lincoln born?
Diagram: Lincoln spoke, and the crowd listened. · Read the speech. · Hurrah! The war ended.
Dictation: "Lincoln spoke for only two minutes, but people still remember his words."
Draft — Change the point of view. Tell the same fable as one of its characters, in the first person and the past tense, as a paragraph.
Lines 1–4 plus the point-of-view line. Clean copy.
If week 31 was a review week, skip this week's A and B (C and D still happen).

weeks.title: Year-end mastery check and the final version

blocks.text: Spread out the five clean copies from weeks 31–35. The child reads each aloud and says which they like best and why. There's no wrong answer.
Longer than a term check: about 40 minutes, and it can be split across two sittings. Answer key below.

The child writes the fable in whichever form they choose (long, short or in a character's voice) or a mix: for example, a paragraph told by a character with some dialogue. Before drafting, the child writes their own four-line checklist from what they've learned this year.

The child revises against their own checklist, makes a fair clean copy for the portfolio, and tells the fable aloud before the family or co-op, alongside Literature's year-end recitation. It's a telling, not a recitation: from memory of the story, not word for word.
Part 1 — Identify (20 items, one point each).
1–8. Name the part of speech of each word in bold: "Oh, the brave boy ran quickly to his mother and told her." (Score eight items: Oh, the, brave, boy, ran, quickly, to, and.)
9. Write the plural of mouse.
10. Write the possessive of children.
11. Choose: Sam and (I / me) went.
12. Underline the verb phrase: "The settlers had planted corn."
13. In "Abe seemed tired," is seemed action or linking?
14. In the same sentence, what is tired?
15. Underline the prepositional phrase: "The cabin stood near the creek."
16. Circle the direct object: "Lincoln wrote a letter."
17. Underline the indirect object: "Lincoln wrote his son a letter."
18. Add the comma: "The river rose but the boat held."
19. Write the future tense of go.
20. Name the kind of sentence: "Hurry to the cabin."
Part 2 — Diagram (8 sentences).
1. The bells rang.
2. Abe was honest.
3. The tall boy read quietly.
4. Lincoln split the rails.
5. The neighbor lent Abe a book.
6. The family lived in a cabin.
7. The war ended, and the country healed.
8. Hurrah! The soldiers came home.
Answer key.

Part 1: 1 Oh, interjection · 2 the, adjective (article) · 3 brave, adjective · 4 boy, noun · 5 ran, verb · 6 quickly, adverb · 7 to, preposition · 8 and, conjunction · 9 mice · 10 children's · 11 I · 12 had planted · 13 linking · 14 predicate adjective · 15 near the creek · 16 letter · 17 son · 18 "rose, but" · 19 will go · 20 imperative.
Part 2:
1. bells | rang; The under bells.
2. Abe | was \ honest.
3. boy | read; The, tall under boy; quietly under read.
4. Lincoln | split | rails; the under rails.
5. neighbor | lent | book; The under neighbor; a under book; Abe on the empty-slant indirect object line under lent.
6. family | lived; The under family; in / cabin (with a) hangs under lived.
7. Two baselines, war | ended (with The) and country | healed (with the), joined by a dotted step labeled and.
8. Hurrah on its own line; soldiers | came, with The under soldiers and home under came.

Year-end mastery standard: 16 of 20 in Part 1 and 6 of 8 in Part 2. This is the Grade 3 grammar exit standard (§3A: "parts of speech mastery, sentence diagramming"). A child below it begins Grade 4 grammar with a review term on the missed topics. Grade 4 extends rather than introduces, so the gap is worth closing first.

after.title: The final version: how to mark it

blocks.text: The final fable is not scored on a rubric. It's the child's own choice of form, judged against their own checklist. The parent writes a short note on the back: one thing the child did well, and one thing to try next time. File it as the last Grade 3 composition.
Fill in this table and file it in the portfolio with the six marked compositions.

For Grade 4: a child who met the mastery standard and wrote steady paragraphs in Terms 4–6 is ready for progymnasmata stage 2 (narrative) and Literature's first formal book reports. A child still writing in sentences, or below the grammar standard, starts Grade 4 there: one more term of fable work and grammar review before stage 2.
Don't let the child switch fables mid-term. Boredom with the chosen fable around week 33 is normal; it's part of the lesson. The final version usually wins it back.
The telling in week 36 matters. Classical rhetoric ends in the spoken word. A child telling a fable well to an audience has done what the progymnasmata was built for.
Celebrate the year. Grade 3 met all eight parts of speech, diagrammed every basic sentence pattern, and climbed the first rung of the ladder. Say so.
Check the Term 5 gate result and decide on a review week
Help the child choose a fable in week 31 and keep one folder for the term's five clean copies
Week 36: give the mastery check (two sittings if needed), hear the telling, and write the note on the final version
Complete the year-end record and file it with the portfolio for Grade 4
